title: Victoria mother hopes for answers at coroner's inquest into son's death
subtitle: 20-year-old Rhett Mutch was shot by police after they were called to his mother's home in 2014
article: For two and a half years Marney Mutch has tried to understand how her call to 911 to get help for her distraught son Rhett ended in his death .
At a coroner's inquest this week, she is hearing about the events firsthand from the officers involved.
"I would like to be able to put the pieces together and to have them fit for me so that I can be at peace," she said.
"I'm just hoping that we do get to a point where I can say okay, let it go."
Mutch called 911 after her son broke into her home on Dallas Road through a basement window on November 1, 2014.
One of the responding officers fatally shot Rhett- and on Tuesday the inquest heard from him.
Const. John Musicco was among several officers who entered the home after Marnie Mutch was brought outside to ensure her safety.
Fighting back tears and taking long breaks to compose himself, Musicco testified that the events happened over the span of just a few minutes.
He said Rhett did not respond to requests from an officer on the other side of the room to put down the knife, and then charged at him and two other officers while still holding the knife.
An officer beside Musicco fired a non-lethal bean bag at Rhett and struck him in the leg, but Musicco said he kept advancing, so he fired a shot from his pistol.
"It was the last option available," he told the inquest.
Musicco said that moments before he fired, he wanted to step back to better assess the situation, but never got the chance.
An earlier independent investigation cleared him of any wrongdoing .
The inquest has also focused on how information was communicated from the 911 operator to the police who responded to the call.
In the 911 call, which was played for the jury, Mutch told the dispatcher that Rhett had a knife, but he wouldn't use it to hurt her. She also told the operator he was holding it by his stomach.
But in a recording of the dispatch audio, a police dispatcher was heard saying Rhett was holding the knife to his throat.
The dispatcher couldn't identify where that information may have come from, and admitted that it could have been his mistake in a chaotic and stressful environment.
Victoria Police Sergeant Gregory Holmes was the supervisor the day of the incident and also testified Monday. He was asked why police responded with force if Mutch wasn't in danger.
Holmes said that he was on his way to the scene when he heard that Rhett had a knife. He said he feared for Mutch's life, but instructed officers to try to negotiate with her son.
He said the officers' first priority was to ensure Mutch was safe and their second priority was to try to intervene and start a dialogue with Rhett.
A seven-person jury is hearing testimony from a range of witnesses. They will then have an opportunity to make recommendations aimed at preventing deaths under similar circumstances.
Mutch, who is representing herself as a participant in the inquest, is scheduled to testify on Wednesday.
